title: Strings
oneLiner: Indexing, slicing and Substring, why strings can't be changed in place, interpolation and formatting, everyday methods, and building strings efficiently with StringBuilder or join.
keyTakeaway: Strings are immutable in both languages: every method that seems to change one returns a new string, so assign the result. Python slices are s[start:end] with the end excluded; C#'s Substring takes (start, length), and its ranges s[start..end] work like Python's. Build a long string from many pieces with StringBuilder in C# or a list plus "".join in Python, not with + in a loop.
explanation:
A string is a piece of text: a sequence of characters such as letters, digits, spaces and punctuation. Almost every program handles text, whether it's names, tag IDs, log lines, file contents or messages from another system, so string handling is where you'll spend a lot of everyday coding time.

Each character in a string has a position, called its index, counting from 0. Indexing reads one character; slicing reads a run of them. The two languages agree on the idea but spell it differently, and the differences (C#'s Substring takes a length, Python quietly clamps a slice that runs off the end) are a steady source of bugs.

Strings are immutable, meaning a string can't be changed once it exists. Upper-casing, trimming or replacing always produces a new string. That makes strings safe to share between parts of a program, but it also means that gluing pieces together with + inside a loop copies the whole string every time, which gets slow for large outputs. Each language has a standard tool for building text efficiently.
